Q: Does an inline constexpr pointer variable guarantee a unique string literal address across translation units? A:

See similar question: C++ standard: ODR and constexpr std::string_view , and similar situation for inline functions (in inline const char* f() { return "abc"; } bool b = (f()==f());, the value of b is unspecified): CWG1823.

The only way this would go wrong is if the One Definition Rule wasn't abided by (Something like inline constexpr const char* p = __DATE__; might fall afoul of this). There is no ODR violation here, since initializer has the same tokens in all TUs, none of the other rules are applicable.

The initializer is evaluated once when the program starts (because it has static storage duration, [basic.start.static]), and test_string would refer to the same object in all translation units. The value is whatever the address of the string-literal happened to be at when it was evaluated at program start, and this initializer is only evaluated once.

Q: JavaScript Execution A:

Yes, pretty much. Machine code is what ultimately gets executed. Any higher level language, including C and JavaScript, must be “translated” (compiled) into machine code eventually. The JavaScript engine is a program that translates JavaScript code into machine executable code on the fly (actually in multiple layers of intermediate translation steps, but that’s an irrelevant detail). That engine itself was originally written in probably some C dialect, yes, and compiled into an executable beforehand (instead of on the fly).
